slides.title: Number algorithms and bits
slides.sub: Chapter 9 · The language of remainders, zeros and ones
slides.main: Numbers in programming live by their own laws: remainders, powers, primes and bits.

captions: Euclid's algorithm and remainder arithmetic are the base for everything else
Fast exponentiation, the sieve of Eratosthenes and prime factorization
Bitwise tricks and iterating over subsets with masks

slides.title: Euclid's algorithm
slides.main: (a, b) → (b, a mod b): steps on the order of log, the last nonzero number is the answer.

captions: Common divisors of a and b are the same as those of b and the remainder a mod b
Replace (a, b) with (b, a mod b): the pair gets smaller
Every two steps the number shrinks at least by half: steps on the order of log
The remainder became zero: the last nonzero number is the answer

slides.title: Extended Euclid
slides.main: Walking backwards we get x and y from a·x + b·y = gcd: the basis of modular inverses.

captions: The same Euclid equalities: we remember the quotients
Going back: 6 = 18 − 1·12
Substitute 12 = 30 − 18 and get 6 = 2·18 − 1·30
Found x and y: 30·(−1) + 18·2 = 6: these are the Bézout coefficients

slides.title: Remainder arithmetic
slides.main: Addition and multiplication can be taken modulo at every step; division is multiplication by the inverse.

captions: Remainders modulo 7 close into a ring
5 + 4 = 9: after taking the remainder we get 2; the remainder can be taken at every step
3 · 5 = 15 ≡ 1: 3 and 5 are mutual inverses, dividing by 3 means multiplying by 5
For prime p: a^(p−1) ≡ 1, so the inverse of a is a^(p−2)

slides.title: Fast exponentiation
slides.main: On the order of log n multiplications instead of n; modulo a number the values don't grow.

captions: 13 = 1101 in binary: the ones stand at places 8, 4 and 1
Square 3 again and again: 3, 9, 81, 6561
Multiply only the powers where the exponent has a one
3¹³ = 6561 · 81 · 3 = 1 594 323: four squarings instead of twelve multiplications

slides.title: Fibonacci in logarithmic time
slides.main: Any linear recurrence is a matrix, and fast exponentiation does the rest.

captions: One multiplication by this matrix advances a pair of Fibonacci numbers by a step
Square it: M² contains F(3), F(2), F(1)
M⁴ is already F(5), F(4), F(3): the exponent doubles
M⁸: the corner holds the Fibonacci number 21, just three matrix multiplications

slides.title: Prime numbers
slides.sub: Trial division up to the root
slides.main: A divisor greater than √n always has a pair smaller than √n: no need to look further.

captions: It is enough to check divisors up to the square root of n
2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 do not divide 91
7 divides 91: the number is composite
The paired divisor 13 is above the root: no need to look for it

frames.text: d and n / d come in pairs: 7 ↔ 13

slides.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes
slides.sub: All primes up to a bound
slides.main: Cross out multiples of a prime starting from its square: time n · log log n.

captions: Wrote the numbers from 2 to 30: all are candidates so far
2 is prime; cross out 4, 6, 8, … all multiples
The next unmarked one is 3; cross out multiples starting from 9
With 5 we start crossing out from 25; the primes are left: 10 numbers

slides.title: Factorization
slides.main: The spf table factors a number in as many steps as it has factors.

captions: The sieve remembers the smallest prime divisor of each number
spf[84] = 2, divide: 42; spf[42] = 2, divide: 21
spf[21] = 3, then 7, and we reach one
84 = 2 · 2 · 3 · 7; the number of divisors is the product of (e + 1)

slides.title: Binomial coefficients modulo a prime
slides.main: C(n, k) = n! · (k!)⁻¹ · ((n − k)!)⁻¹: constant time after preparation.

captions: Compute the factorials modulo once
Inverse factorials: one by Fermat power, the rest by walking backwards
1 · 4 · 6 = 24 ≡ 3, and 10 mod 7 = 3: it matches

slides.title: Bitwise tricks
slides.main: x & (x − 1) clears the lowest one; x & −x leaves only it.

captions: 44 in binary: 00101100: the lowest one is in the third place from the right
x − 1 flips the lowest one and the zeros below it
x & (x − 1) clears the lowest one: we got 40
x & −x leaves only the lowest one: we got 4

slides.title: Subset masks
slides.main: All subsets are a loop over numbers from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; submasks: s = (s − 1) & mask.

captions: A set of three elements is the numbers from 0 to 7: bit i means «a, b, c included»
Mask 101 is the subset {a, c}
The answer for every mask is dynamic programming over subsets: 2ⁿ states

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Remainders, powers, primes and bits are a set of techniques that come up in problems all the time.

captions: Euclid, modular inverses and fast exponentiation: the language of remainders
The sieve, the divisor table and factorials give primes and binomials
Masks turn subsets into numbers and speed up iteration
